svg.text: PowerMonger economy: what moves a lord's food, men, goods and loyalty
Everything that changes one lord's four numbers, and which routine or order changes it (the lord record, $4e514, 32 bytes)
PowerMonger (Bullfrog / Electronic Arts, 1990, here the Atari ST version) is a war game on a height-mapped land of settlements. This
figure comes from reverse-engineering the game's 68000 machine code (the ST's CPU) and running it in an emulator. Each settlement belongs
to a lord, and each lord has a 32-byte record holding four things the player has to manage: his food store, his men at home, eight goods
counters and a loyalty pressure that turns the lord to another side when it reaches 600. The armies the player and the computer lords
command are captains' groups that take food, men and goods from their lords.
There is no economy routine that grows a population or balances food once per period. Every change to those four numbers is a single write
made by one man's state-machine handler (his "mode", a byte saying what he is doing, written $xx) or by an order. In winter, farmers,
merchants and fishers "park" at home and each periodic "pulse" then charges the lord for them. The figure collects every such write for
one lord record: the civilians who fill it on the left, the record in the middle, the armies that draw on it on the right.
$ numbers are addresses in the game's memory, given as citations; the text says what each one is. Evidence: proven = checked against the game's own code with
a match count; observed = seen in the running game; inferred = read from the code or reasoned, not run.

svg.text: How to read it
Middle: the lord record, one box per field, named by its byte offset in the record (+6 is byte 6). Left: civilian men in their job modes. Right: the
army, a captain's group record and its men. Each arrow is one kind of write: an arrow into the middle adds to the field, an arrow out of it subtracts,
a pair of arrows does both. The label on the arrow is the change per event; "share" is the fraction of a store an order moves, set by the group's
posture (its aggression setting: 2 aggressive takes all, 3 neutral half, 4 passive a quarter). The first line of each box names the event; the routine
or mode that makes the write follows as a citation; the fill is the evidence for that flow.
What to take from it
Food. Food comes in only from fishermen (+4 a catch) and farmers coming home (+2). It leaves to armies, to gatherers whose delivery has no group, and
to the winter upkeep, one per parked man per pulse.
Men. Men are conserved: every arrow on the men field moves one man between the lord, a group or another lord, and none is born after the world build
(observed over traced runs, not proven absent). The pigeon landing is the one path that adds a man without taking him from elsewhere: it revives a
dead man's record.
Goods. Goods come in one at a time from felled trees, heavily throttled, and are spent by armies to equip and upgrade their men. What the game calls
"invention" (the weapon grade of its men) is that upgrade, not a research timer. Men and goods are separate ledgers: goods never become men, and food
and goods meet only in the trade.
Loyalty. A lord's towns that go hungry in winter push his loyalty pressure up; at 600 he and his settlements change side and the pressure resets to
300. This is the game's own clock, not something the player triggers.
Terms and evidence
The share is computed as a bit shift: shift = posture - 2 ($30fe), so an order moves food >> shift (aggressive all, neutral half, passive a quarter).
36(group) is the group's own food, which the captain panel labels "Food:". Men at home are the lord's men, not in an army. The winter park (mode $7c)
needs the season word $57fd0 == 0: farmers ($16), merchants ($4e) and fishers ($5e) park there, so upkeep and loyalty move only in winter (a man
idling in $7e pulses too, never on that first-pulse edge). Mission 1 builds both enemy lords at 608; the first winter pulse resets them to 300.
Proven means checked against the game's own code: a Python rewrite of the routine was run beside the game's own 68000 code from many saved game states
and every changed byte matched (18452/18452 is matching bytes out of bytes compared). Observed means seen in the running game and counted: "live: town
22 -> 11" is one run in which a town's food went from 22 to 11; "one run, land 5, 100M steps" is a saved game state on land 5 run for 100 million
emulated instructions. Inferred means read from the disassembly only.
Evidence:
proven (checked against the game's own code)
observed (seen in the running game)
inferred (read from the code, not run)
